full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll start by telling you a bit about what we’re doing. We’re basically interviewing women from across all the engineering disciplines mainly who are about to go on their placement, but we are interviewing some people that aren’t going on placement as well. Are you going on the placement?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah

Interviewer:	We’re looking at why women choose to do engineering and what they expect to get from their placement and why they want to do the placement. And we’re looking at how that differs when people actually get on their placement, how that affects their career intentions and so on and what we’re trying to do is put together a practical guidance document to give to the engineering councils to say how they can help retain women and get more numbers of women into the industry (yes). If I can start by asking you just a few background questions really – you’re doing civil engineering, aren’t you?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you do A levels?

Subject:	Er, no I had my high school in Canada.

Interviewer:	Oh right, Ok. 

Subject:	Erm, and eventually I went to the States to start my university but I didn’t quite like it and I was there for only one quarter so – and then I went to (lost words) in Hong Kong and they give me an offer straight away, so I think maybe I give it a try.

Interviewer:	OK, when you were in America were you doing engineering still?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK. What type of school did you go to, before you went to university? Was it an all girls school or anything like that?

Subject:	It’s kind of private high school (right) in Canada.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got any other work experience, in the industry, or other work experience?

Subject:	I do have work experience but it’s not related to engineering.

Interviewer:	Right, OK. What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	No, my father is a businessman – well he has a shipping company and he runs it. And my mother she – she was helping my grandfather’s business but now she’s a housewife

Interviewer:	OK, have you travelled about quite a bit then?

Subject:	Yeah, been all over.

Interviewer:	How long have you been in the UK then? Did you come over when you came to University?

Subject:	Yes, so this is my 2nd year or 1 year and a half to be precise.

Interviewer:	Are your family in the UK as well?

Subject:	No they’re in Hong Kong.

Interviewer:	Right, so I’m going to ask you a bit about why you decided to do engineering now. Is there any particular things, that stand out in your mind, why you chose engineering?

Subject:	Er, cos I don’t feel that I can do business. When I see my father running a business, I find it quite hard er there’s not really a regular schedule. When anything goes wrong you have to go straight away. Probably it’s the same with engineering but I – I’d rather take the responsibility of engineering. And I found that more – erm satisfying things in engineering because I’d like to say I did this bridge, or something. I find it – yes.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider doing anything else like maybe social sciences or something like that?

Subject:	I’d love to do politics and literature, but since I don’t apply to Hong Kong, after I’ve graduated I don’t think it’s easy for me to have a career on that path.

Interviewer:	OK, so you think that once you’ve finished your education, because you’ve done engineering you’ll be in quite a good position to get a job.

Subject:	I think I can travel quite a bit and this is more since engineering, I think, more than similar. So then I can hopefully get a job where I want.

Interviewer:	Ok did any other factors influence your decision to take up engineering – has your family been supportive?

Subject:	Mm, no. Actually it was a friend of mine. I was thinking to do science subjects and he said he’s studying about engineering and that idea came across my mind and I started to think it could be a good idea. My family, they are neutral – my mother actually said it could be quite tough for a girl to do civil engineering, but, I think, or yeah, I’d like – yeah, I think I’d like the course so…and engineering discipline can go to business sector as well.

Interviewer:	Did you do much research into what engineering is? Did you know any other engineers to speak to? To find out what it’s all about?

Subject:	You mean for Civil?

Interviewer:	Well how did you decide to do civil and say not mechanical engineering?

Subject:	Er, because mechanical – they’re building bridges.

Interviewer:	So you like that side of it?

Subject:	I like the infrastructure, I think. I was thinking to do materials as well but I decided to do civil, that’s all.

Interviewer:	OK, did you always know that you’d like to do the sandwich course?

Subject:	From when they tell me, I decided to do it, yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider going to any other universities?

Subject:	Erm, yeah. I was in another university already. [University] and [university], they give me an offer but ‘cos [this university] gave me the first place, so I thought [this university].

Interviewer:	OK, when you started in engineering, did you realise that there weren’t many women in engineering?

Subject:	I knew that, right from the beginning.

Interviewer:	Did it bother you at all?

Subject:	No, they are quite friendly so it’s OK.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I’d say engineering (?) could be quite tough. I wouldn’t say encourage or discourage but it would be helpful if women know more about engineering because after all it’s a personal decision.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that there maybe aren’t more women in engineering because they don’t actually know what engineering is in the first place? They need more information.

Subject:	Er, to be honest I think – because engineering is quite a heavy workload subject and erm that – not really a very attractive point. They might want more information but I think if we are willing to do the research, we can get more – there’s some ideas. But it would be nice if there was some support.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, well ones who work hard and are responsible. Good communication skills, good listening skills in team work – decision making.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those things are particularly male or female?

Subject:	Erm, I think somehow male and female can manage these in a different way. Erm, you know, when we work in a team – well if they are your friends that will be OK, if they are not – sometimes I find it a bit difficult to interact with them. Er, I’ve never had group mate – a female group mate, that I don’t know well, so I don’t know how that works with them.

Interviewer:	Er, OK. Do you think that there any advantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Er, yes. Sometimes, doing heavy steelwork they will let you go. (laughter) Maybe I don’t have to weld it, I just hold it or some easier task.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

Subject:	Yeah, they might consider that you are – they will do, because it might be too hard for you, but I can do it.

Interviewer:	OK, I’d like to ask you a few things about the course now. Has the course at [this university] been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Yeah, I really like it.

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think have been the best and worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	It’s just I think I’ve learned a lot more but at first I didn’t know what to expect from the course. So everything’s quite a surprise and new for me. But I like it. Some modules they are quite boring and er, coursework they are quite hard but most of all I find it quite interesting and the lecturers they are willing to – to teach and they are patient.

Interviewer:	How does it compare to the course that you were doing before?

Subject:	You mean in the USA?

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you like it better?

Subject:	I didn’t really like the atmosphere in that university or the situation (?). I don’t find it very friendly. The people are OK but the city, overall, I don’t find it – I can’t see myself living there for the – for 6 years. Er, it takes too long to complete a course. They told me it probably takes 5 years to complete an engineering course with sandwich.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	How many?

Subject:	I have one.

Interviewer:	Just one. Do you think that there’s any difference in the style of teaching between the male and the female lecturers?

Subject:	I think the male lecturers tend to go faster you know – at a faster pace. Erm, and I think my female lecturer got a special way to lecture, so it’s quite hard to compare.

Interviewer:	OK, do you find it encouraging, having a female lecturer? Do you think there should be more female lecturers?

Subject:	Hmm, I don’t mind to have male or female lecturers as long as they are able to teach.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the female lecturer treated you more or less the same as the males?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Do you have a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yes, I do.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	Male.

Interviewer:	Do you mind that they’re male? Would you prefer a female personal tutor?

Subject:	I don’t mind at all.

Interviewer:	Would you be happy going to them, for anything?

Subject:	Yeah, because what I go for is academic, so male or female could be the same.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s good. Who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started your degree?

Subject:	Biggest influence? My friend, I think, I met a lot of new people, when I came to university. And lecturers as well.

Interviewer:	Has that helped you?

Subject:	Yes, I think I’ve become a different person, or a stronger person.

Interviewer:	OK, you have said earlier about group work, do you have to do much group and team work?

Subject:	Yes, we do.

Interviewer:	OK, do you get to choose who you want to work with generally or are you put into groups?

Subject:	Er, sometimes, with a certain project, we can choose. But the lab work, it’s fixed.

Interviewer:	OK, do you prefer choosing yourself, or do you mind being put in groups?

Subject:	I prefer choosing myself.

Interviewer:	When you do choose yourself, how do you choose who you want to work with?

Subject:	Erm, I just stick with my usual group of friends.

Interviewer:	OK, is that group mainly men or women?

Subject:	A mix of both.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you like it being a mix?

Subject:	Er, it could be nice and well, they are my friends, so I don’t mind at all. But sometimes there’s another female there who’s got (lost words through laughter)

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm, sometimes my group mate will not turn up on time or they just disappeared. It’s quite annoying sometimes.

Interviewer:	Is it worse when you’re working with people you know or worse when you’re working with people you don’t know.

Subject:	With people I don’t know because I can’t – well I think everyone finds it easier to communicate with people you already know.

Interviewer:	Yeah, when you’re working in the groups, with people you don’t know, do the men treat the women differently at all, to how they treat each other, do you think?

Subject:	Er, I think they are quite fair on the mental work. On the physical work they might help you.

Interviewer:	OK, what parts of the university teaching and advice that you’ve had, do you think will help you when you go on placement?

Subject:	In which part?

Interviewer:	What sort of skills do you think that you’ll take from the course to the placement.

Subject:	Erm, I’d say personal skills sometimes and depends on where am I going to placement. If I go on contractor, then it will be some practical surveying skills, or if I go onto consultancy then it will be some design things that – personal skills.

Interviewer:	OK, have you applied to many different companies?

Subject:	I think around 12 or 14.

Interviewer:	OK – you’re waiting to hear from them, at the minute?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any skills from your previous work experience that you might take with you onto the placement?

Subject:	Personal skills again.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on placement, at the minute?

Subject:	Mm, not really because I don’t really know what to expect from placement.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university should help you prepare a bit more?

Subject:	Er, they do help us. Sometimes they can’t – they try to let you know, such as it’s a totally new experience that you’ll never expect…

Interviewer:	OK, do you think the way you are taught, and being at university, reflects what it’s going to be like when you go out to work in the industry?

Subject:	I guess it will be quite different. But first there are the fundamental things we have to know, so I guess we have to know it. And, for the industry, I think – I think it will be more into business rather than doing just pure civil engineering.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you decide that you wanted to go on a placement?

Subject:	Because I want some experiences in the civil industry and hopefully I can get the job easier after I graduate.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will improve your career prospects?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think there’s any reason for people to choose not to go on a placement?

Subject:	Some of them don’t – like to finish the course earlier, and carry on another course. Or they want to leave university and go into the real world earlier.

Interviewer:	OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

Subject:	My Dad told me not to go on placement. Yeah, he thinks it’s better to finish university earlier but I believe it’s better to have some experience.

Interviewer:	Ok, you weren’t too influenced by what your father …?

Subject:	I argue with him.

Interviewer:	How did you decide on the types of companies that you’ve applied to?

Subject:	Erm, I’m applying to big companies (yes) because I like to travel around but I want to have something with company so that it looks better on my CV. And I will have experience working in the big company.

Interviewer:	Did you say that you’ve applied to some consultancies and to some construction type...?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	So you aren’t too bothered, at the minute, which of those that you’re going to or do you have a preference?

Subject:	I would prefer to go into contracting. But then I am thinking, I don’t know if I can handle the situations on site and it’s – it would be a more relaxing environment, in consultancy. So I applied to contractors in the first place and then I applied to consultants.

Interviewer:	Oh right, OK. When you were applying to companies, did you look at things like pay and maybe training opportunities and whether you could get a job at the end of it, or anything like that?

Subject:	I tried to look at it but most of the companies don’t mention anything about that. But they generally offer opportunity and I’ve found most of the companies they do provide quite a large range.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much research into all of the companies?

Subject:	Yes, quite a lot. 

Interviewer:	And where did you find the information that you got?

Subject:	Where?

Interviewer:	Where abouts did you get that?

Subject:	From the Internet, from the Hobsons Guides and from Prospects and everything.

Interviewer:	OK, have the university been very helpful in helping you find the placement?

Subject:	Erm, they –they give us an email when they are coming – coming in for presentations. And I do think the tutor is working hard on it and he is trying to get everybody into the industry.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think there is anything else that they could do to help you?

Subject:	Erm, I know that some girl in the department, they almost go and get you a job, but I think it’s a very good experience when you are to go on an interview yourself, for the real experience, rather than getting you a job. So I think it’s…

Interviewer:	The whole experience?

Subject:	Yes, my tutor he’s been – done very well.

Interviewer:	OK, what – what sort of skills and things like that do you think that you’ll get out of going on placement?

Subject:	First of all I know what civil engineering is really like. Erm, some technical skills because being on site for a year will be – probably will learn more than staying on at university and yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think – what will be the best and worst of like going on placement?

Subject:	The best thing is to get (?). To know more people and to larger your network and know what to expect after you graduate, when you go into work. The bad side is it’s very hard to handle the situation at times, I think, especially on site because I really have no idea what will happen there.

Interviewer:	Ok, you’re worried about that?

Subject:	I think there will probably be kind to us in the first few weeks, but hopefully it will be OK.

Interviewer:	How did you think that work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	Work and university?

Interviewer:	Yes.

Subject:	First of all, I have to get up early. Erm, and university has got extra responsibilities and course work to do, after school, which for work, you might do overtime but you don’t have to give – it’s stressful, but it’s different kind of stress and different kind of schedule and different life.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you mean like when you get home in the evenings, that will be it, you won’t have any more work to do whereas at university you’re probably doing coursework and things like that?

Subject:	Erm, I’d say after work you can do extra work but not compulsory, it’s according to your own preference or your working schedule, whereas university, because there is certain coursework that you have to hand in, so you definitely have to do it. Erm, and timetable is different. While other university students can go out every night, I was in (?) with (?) work I can do.

Interviewer:	Are you looking forward to that side of it, or not, really?

Subject:	Not really, no.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, where do you think that you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	Er, I hope that I can be Chartered, or I’ll carry on and an MSc programme after the undergraduate.

Interviewer:	Do you think you do want to be an engineer or are you hoping that the placement might help you make up your mind about what you want to do?

Subject:	No, I do think I want to be an engineer, but I don’t know if I want to be consultant or contractor. And I think my placement experience will help me make the decision.

Interviewer:	OK, what about more long term, say in 10 years time, what do you think you’ll be doing?

Subject:	Definitely being chartered. Hopefully I can be senior engineer or be responsible for quite large project and I can travel around.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think would be your ideal career?

Subject:	Civil Engineer.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there’ll be any problems or difficulties trying to become a civil engineer at all?

Subject:	At the moment, I don’t – I can’t think of any.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s good. Do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I wouldn’t imagine it is hard to have a job but I really think that the salary is not very competitive (OK) because engineers are – they put in a lot of hard work. Erm, the starting salary’s good but after being a senior engineer, it’s not going very far.

Interviewer:	Do you think that once you get a job in the industry, there are opportunities for you to go further – like to be managing people and doing things like that?

Subject:	Er, there might be eventually, if I carry on probably for a few years time.

Interviewer:	OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

Subject:	No, I wouldn’t – I’m happy with it.

Interviewer:	OK, would you maybe have come straight here instead of going to America, or are you pleased that you went to…?

Subject:	Very pleased that I’m in [this university].

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that going to America, helped you appreciate being in [this university] more?

Subject:	Yeah – I was in America a few years ago before I went to Canada. Er, and going back to America I find it very different and that it’s not what I like. So being in [this university] gives me a different experience, which I prefer.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of engineering?

Subject:	Erm, analytical, to analyse. Group work, problem solving erm hard work and brilliant.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

Subject:	A little bit yes. 

Interviewer:	What do you think that is?

Subject:	Obviously some days I’m having metalwork and concrete work and it’s more problem solving and to analyse, which gives me that impression.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think the situation will improve, as more women are going into the industry?

Subject:	Do you mean the impression of masculine?

Interviewer:	Yes.

Subject:	I think it’s the characteristic of the subject itself rather than the proportion of female and male.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any aspects of the engineering culture might be problematic for you?

Subject:	Er, business. Construction management – it’s a bit hard.

Interviewer:	Do you think the fact that it is so masculine will be a problem at all?

Subject:	Er, no. This is what I expected.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that your educational experiences differ at all from people doing other subjects like Social Sciences and business and things like that?

Subject:	Very different.

Interviewer:	Why’s that?

Subject:	Er, I’d say to the way engineer thinks and the way that people do in business or social courses thinks are different.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that’s a good thing?

Subject:	For me personally, I think that it is.

Interviewer:	Do you think that is just because of the type of subjects that the students take?

Subject:	It could be. I believe that people are trained up to think in a certain way. Thinking in an engineering way, it’s more fundamental and problem solving – we’re more realistic.

Interviewer:	OK, well that’s everything I have to ask you. Thank you very much for taking part.

Subject:	And being a civil engineer, you might travel quite a bit and it’s very hard work but you might have to concentrate in your career totally, well having a family you have responsibility for your family and then I guess every female does – you start to think which is more important. And if you think your career is taking up too much time, then probably you might leave it. Or probably more simple, if you’re in contractor and if you’re pregnant, you just won’t go on site, and then after you leave for a year, then you probably just let go.

Interviewer:	Do you think it is a particular problem with the engineering industry, the fact that you’re in an industry which is particularly difficult to combine having a family and working because of long hours and travelling and things like that?

Subject:	Erm, don’t know I think it depends on personalities and what the individuals think. But I think contractor will be a disadvantage to having a females in there, especially after they’re married.

Interviewer:	Yeah, when you’ve been trying to decide whether to do the contracting or the consultancy have you been thinking about things like that or is it not an issue at the minute?

Subject:	Not at the moment but eventually I think I’ll go into consulting because I wouldn’t imagine myself, at age 40, climbing up and down (laughter)

Interviewer:	OK, that’s great thank you.

turns.text: No, they are quite friendly so it’s OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’d say engineering (?) could be quite tough. I wouldn’t say encourage or discourage but it would be helpful if women know more about engineering because after all it’s a personal decision.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that there maybe aren’t more women in engineering because they don’t actually know what engineering is in the first place? They need more information.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, to be honest I think – because engineering is quite a heavy workload subject and erm that – not really a very attractive point. They might want more information but I think if we are willing to do the research, we can get more – there’s some ideas. But it would be nice if there was some support.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well ones who work hard and are responsible. Good communication skills, good listening skills in team work – decision making.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those things are particularly male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think somehow male and female can manage these in a different way. Erm, you know, when we work in a team – well if they are your friends that will be OK, if they are not – sometimes I find it a bit difficult to interact with them. Er, I’ve never had group mate – a female group mate, that I don’t know well, so I don’t know how that works with them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Er, OK. Do you think that there any advantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes. Sometimes, doing heavy steelwork they will let you go. (laughter) Maybe I don’t have to weld it, I just hold it or some easier task.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they might consider that you are – they will do, because it might be too hard for you, but I can do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I’d like to ask you a few things about the course now. Has the course at [this university] been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I really like it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think have been the best and worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s just I think I’ve learned a lot more but at first I didn’t know what to expect from the course. So everything’s quite a surprise and new for me. But I like it. Some modules they are quite boring and er, coursework they are quite hard but most of all I find it quite interesting and the lecturers they are willing to – to teach and they are patient.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How does it compare to the course that you were doing before?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You mean in the USA?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you like it better?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I didn’t really like the atmosphere in that university or the situation (?). I don’t find it very friendly. The people are OK but the city, overall, I don’t find it – I can’t see myself living there for the – for 6 years. Er, it takes too long to complete a course. They told me it probably takes 5 years to complete an engineering course with sandwich.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Just one. Do you think that there’s any difference in the style of teaching between the male and the female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the male lecturers tend to go faster you know – at a faster pace. Erm, and I think my female lecturer got a special way to lecture, so it’s quite hard to compare.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you find it encouraging, having a female lecturer? Do you think there should be more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I don’t mind to have male or female lecturers as long as they are able to teach.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the female lecturer treated you more or less the same as the males?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you mind that they’re male? Would you prefer a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t mind at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you be happy going to them, for anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because what I go for is academic, so male or female could be the same.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s good. Who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started your degree?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Biggest influence? My friend, I think, I met a lot of new people, when I came to university. And lecturers as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that helped you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think I’ve become a different person, or a stronger person.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you have said earlier about group work, do you have to do much group and team work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, we do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you get to choose who you want to work with generally or are you put into groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, sometimes, with a certain project, we can choose. But the lab work, it’s fixed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you prefer choosing yourself, or do you mind being put in groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I prefer choosing myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you do choose yourself, how do you choose who you want to work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I just stick with my usual group of friends.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is that group mainly men or women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A mix of both.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you like it being a mix?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it could be nice and well, they are my friends, so I don’t mind at all. But sometimes there’s another female there who’s got (lost words through laughter)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, sometimes my group mate will not turn up on time or they just disappeared. It’s quite annoying sometimes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it worse when you’re working with people you know or worse when you’re working with people you don’t know.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: With people I don’t know because I can’t – well I think everyone finds it easier to communicate with people you already know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, when you’re working in the groups, with people you don’t know, do the men treat the women differently at all, to how they treat each other, do you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think they are quite fair on the mental work. On the physical work they might help you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what parts of the university teaching and advice that you’ve had, do you think will help you when you go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In which part?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of skills do you think that you’ll take from the course to the placement.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’d say personal skills sometimes and depends on where am I going to placement. If I go on contractor, then it will be some practical surveying skills, or if I go onto consultancy then it will be some design things that – personal skills.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you applied to many different companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think around 12 or 14.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK – you’re waiting to hear from them, at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any skills from your previous work experience that you might take with you onto the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Personal skills again.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel prepared and ready to go on placement, at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, not really because I don’t really know what to expect from placement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university should help you prepare a bit more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, they do help us. Sometimes they can’t – they try to let you know, such as it’s a totally new experience that you’ll never expect…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think the way you are taught, and being at university, reflects what it’s going to be like when you go out to work in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I guess it will be quite different. But first there are the fundamental things we have to know, so I guess we have to know it. And, for the industry, I think – I think it will be more into business rather than doing just pure civil engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you decide that you wanted to go on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because I want some experiences in the civil industry and hopefully I can get the job easier after I graduate.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will improve your career prospects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think there’s any reason for people to choose not to go on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Some of them don’t – like to finish the course earlier, and carry on another course. Or they want to leave university and go into the real world earlier.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did anyone particularly encourage you or discourage you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My Dad told me not to go on placement. Yeah, he thinks it’s better to finish university earlier but I believe it’s better to have some experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, you weren’t too influenced by what your father …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I argue with him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide on the types of companies that you’ve applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’m applying to big companies (yes) because I like to travel around but I want to have something with company so that it looks better on my CV. And I will have experience working in the big company.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you say that you’ve applied to some consultancies and to some construction type...?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you aren’t too bothered, at the minute, which of those that you’re going to or do you have a preference?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would prefer to go into contracting. But then I am thinking, I don’t know if I can handle the situations on site and it’s – it would be a more relaxing environment, in consultancy. So I applied to contractors in the first place and then I applied to consultants.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh right, OK. When you were applying to companies, did you look at things like pay and maybe training opportunities and whether you could get a job at the end of it, or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I tried to look at it but most of the companies don’t mention anything about that. But they generally offer opportunity and I’ve found most of the companies they do provide quite a large range.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much research into all of the companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, quite a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And where did you find the information that you got?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Where?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Where abouts did you get that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: From the Internet, from the Hobsons Guides and from Prospects and everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have the university been very helpful in helping you find the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, they –they give us an email when they are coming – coming in for presentations. And I do think the tutor is working hard on it and he is trying to get everybody into the industry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think there is anything else that they could do to help you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I know that some girl in the department, they almost go and get you a job, but I think it’s a very good experience when you are to go on an interview yourself, for the real experience, rather than getting you a job. So I think it’s…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The whole experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, my tutor he’s been – done very well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what – what sort of skills and things like that do you think that you’ll get out of going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: First of all I know what civil engineering is really like. Erm, some technical skills because being on site for a year will be – probably will learn more than staying on at university and yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think – what will be the best and worst of like going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best thing is to get (?). To know more people and to larger your network and know what to expect after you graduate, when you go into work. The bad side is it’s very hard to handle the situation at times, I think, especially on site because I really have no idea what will happen there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, you’re worried about that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there will probably be kind to us in the first few weeks, but hopefully it will be OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you think that work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Work and university?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: First of all, I have to get up early. Erm, and university has got extra responsibilities and course work to do, after school, which for work, you might do overtime but you don’t have to give – it’s stressful, but it’s different kind of stress and different kind of schedule and different life.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you mean like when you get home in the evenings, that will be it, you won’t have any more work to do whereas at university you’re probably doing coursework and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I’d say after work you can do extra work but not compulsory, it’s according to your own preference or your working schedule, whereas university, because there is certain coursework that you have to hand in, so you definitely have to do it. Erm, and timetable is different. While other university students can go out every night, I was in (?) with (?) work I can do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you looking forward to that side of it, or not, really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, where do you think that you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I hope that I can be Chartered, or I’ll carry on and an MSc programme after the undergraduate.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you do want to be an engineer or are you hoping that the placement might help you make up your mind about what you want to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I do think I want to be an engineer, but I don’t know if I want to be consultant or contractor. And I think my placement experience will help me make the decision.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about more long term, say in 10 years time, what do you think you’ll be doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely being chartered. Hopefully I can be senior engineer or be responsible for quite large project and I can travel around.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think would be your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Civil Engineer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there’ll be any problems or difficulties trying to become a civil engineer at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At the moment, I don’t – I can’t think of any.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s good. Do you think that the career prospects are good in your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I wouldn’t imagine it is hard to have a job but I really think that the salary is not very competitive (OK) because engineers are – they put in a lot of hard work. Erm, the starting salary’s good but after being a senior engineer, it’s not going very far.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that once you get a job in the industry, there are opportunities for you to go further – like to be managing people and doing things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, there might be eventually, if I carry on probably for a few years time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently if you had to do it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I wouldn’t – I’m happy with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you maybe have come straight here instead of going to America, or are you pleased that you went to…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very pleased that I’m in [this university].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that going to America, helped you appreciate being in [this university] more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – I was in America a few years ago before I went to Canada. Er, and going back to America I find it very different and that it’s not what I like. So being in [this university] gives me a different experience, which I prefer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, analytical, to analyse. Group work, problem solving erm hard work and brilliant.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the engineering culture is masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A little bit yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think that is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Obviously some days I’m having metalwork and concrete work and it’s more problem solving and to analyse, which gives me that impression.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think the situation will improve, as more women are going into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Do you mean the impression of masculine?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s the characteristic of the subject itself rather than the proportion of female and male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any aspects of the engineering culture might be problematic for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, business. Construction management – it’s a bit hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the fact that it is so masculine will be a problem at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, no. This is what I expected.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that your educational experiences differ at all from people doing other subjects like Social Sciences and business and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why’s that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I’d say to the way engineer thinks and the way that people do in business or social courses thinks are different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that’s a good thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: For me personally, I think that it is.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that is just because of the type of subjects that the students take?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It could be. I believe that people are trained up to think in a certain way. Thinking in an engineering way, it’s more fundamental and problem solving – we’re more realistic.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, well that’s everything I have to ask you. Thank you very much for taking part.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And being a civil engineer, you might travel quite a bit and it’s very hard work but you might have to concentrate in your career totally, well having a family you have responsibility for your family and then I guess every female does – you start to think which is more important. And if you think your career is taking up too much time, then probably you might leave it. Or probably more simple, if you’re in contractor and if you’re pregnant, you just won’t go on site, and then after you leave for a year, then you probably just let go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it is a particular problem with the engineering industry, the fact that you’re in an industry which is particularly difficult to combine having a family and working because of long hours and travelling and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, don’t know I think it depends on personalities and what the individuals think. But I think contractor will be a disadvantage to having a females in there, especially after they’re married.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, when you’ve been trying to decide whether to do the contracting or the consultancy have you been thinking about things like that or is it not an issue at the minute?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not at the moment but eventually I think I’ll go into consulting because I wouldn’t imagine myself, at age 40, climbing up and down (laughter)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s great thank you.
